newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC meeting says size not might in open economy.
newsitem.headline: APEC meeting says size not might in open economy.

text.p: An open intra-regional trade and investment regime does not spell doom for small enterprises but offers them opportunities to thrive, APEC trade officials said this weekend.

Philip Lader, chief U.S. delegate to a meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, said size should not be an issue when APEC economies open up in the next 14 to 24 years in line with an agreed timetable.

The Cebu conference was the third ministerial meeting held by APEC members on small and medium sized enterprises (SMEs) ahead of a summit meeting of APEC leaders to be held in November in the Philippines.
"The growth of the SMEs will (depend on) the fire in the bellies of the entrepreneurs themselves," Lader, head of the U.S. Small Business Administration, told reporters.
"Some will seek to keep relatively small businesses because that's what they want to do. But they will improve their market niche, their profitability."
APEC officials attribute the strong growth of most APEC members to SMEs, many of which account for 30 to 80 percent of their countries' gross domestic products.
Under the APEC agenda, all trade and investment opportunities should be made available to big and small corporations without special favour to fledgling companies.
Despite this, Taiwanese Trade Minister Shien-Chien Yang said he foresaw that the role of the SMEs in APEC economies would be as crucial in the coming years as it was today.
"You will see large companies will grow from (today's) SMEs... (but) you will see many, many more young entrepreneurs starting up their companies (as well)," he said.

The trade ministers agreed at the end of their two-day Cebu meeting to facilitate freer flow of market information, work out innovative financing schemes and provide technology transfer among small businesses to harness their competitiveness.
The proposals will form part of the SME action agenda to be endorsed to the APEC summit.
Philippine Trade Secretary Cesar Bautista, the conference's chairman, said small businesses had their innate edge of flexibility and creativity to deal with changing market trends and demands.
"Many of the successes of big corporations are not because of the skills of big corporations but due to the skills of smaller enterprises working with them," Bautista said.
"We have to empower these SMEs to...be more confident of their capabilities when they deal with the global economy."
Canadian Industry Minister John Manley viewed the pending globalisation of the economies as an opportunity to help small businesses prosper.
"The amount of opportunities that the internationalisation of the market is bringing (to) the small firms...is what will define the role of the SMEs in the 21st century," he said.
With freer access to technology information, SMEs could be the driving economic force in the next century, he said.

APEC members are Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Philippines, Chinese Taipei, Thailand, Singapore, and the United States.
